analogy.p: Imagine organising a school trip. **Abstraction** is ignoring things that do not matter for the plan, such as the colour of the coach, and keeping the things that do, like date, cost and number of students. **Decomposition** is splitting the trip into jobs: transport, permission slips, money, food and risk assessment, each given to a different teacher. **Algorithmic thinking** is writing the exact sequence for each job, such as send letter, collect forms, count the replies, book the coach. The analogy breaks down because a person can cope with vague instructions like 'sort out lunch', whereas a computer needs every step spelled out precisely.

bullets: Three principles to know: **abstraction, decomposition, algorithmic thinking**.
Computational thinking happens **before** programming, during the design stage.
A **computer** can only follow precise instructions, so the problem must first be made precise.
The same skills help with **non-computing problems**, such as planning a school trip.
Typical exam wording: 'Explain what is meant by...' or 'Describe how ... could be used to...'.
Link to other topics: the results feed into **pseudocode and flowcharts**, **trace tables**, and **programming constructs** in later sections of Paper 2.
Always **define first, then apply** to the scenario given.
core.p: **Computational thinking** is the set of problem-solving skills used to turn a real problem into something a computer can solve. It is not about typing code; it is about **thinking** clearly before any code is written. The OCR J277 specification names three principles you must know: **abstraction**, **decomposition** and **algorithmic thinking**. Used together, they let you take a large, messy problem, strip it down to what matters, split it into manageable pieces and then work out the exact steps needed to solve each piece. Exam questions often ask you to explain what each principle means and to show it in a given scenario.

bullets: Abstraction = **hide or remove unnecessary detail** and focus on what is important.
Produces a **simplified model** of the real-world problem.
Requires deciding what is **relevant** to the task and what can be ignored.
Makes the problem **easier to understand and solve**, and the program shorter and simpler.
It is **not** the same as breaking the problem into parts (that is decomposition).
Exam phrase: 'removing unnecessary detail so only the important features are considered'.
Higher marks: say **why** the detail is not needed in the given scenario.
core.p: **Abstraction** is the process of **removing or hiding unnecessary detail** so that you focus only on the information that is needed to solve the problem. The result is a simpler **model** or representation of the real situation. You decide which details are **relevant** and which can be ignored. Abstraction makes a problem easier to understand, easier to solve and easier to program, because the programmer does not have to deal with every real-world complication at once. A good abstraction keeps everything that matters and removes everything that does not.

bullets: **Transport map**: shows stations and connections, not the true geography (see the figure).
**Satnav/route planner**: shows the road ahead, hides irrelevant streets and buildings.
**Game character**: represented by data such as position, speed and health, not every physical detail.
**Variables** and **functions** hide the details of values and processes behind names.
**User interface**: a button labelled 'Print' hides the complex steps the computer performs.
**Data structure**: a list of names is an abstraction of data stored in memory locations.
Always explain **what was removed** and **what was kept**.
core.p: The classic example is a **map**. A route map for travelling between stations shows the stops and the order in which they come, but leaves out the exact shape of the track, the buildings, trees and distances because a passenger does not need them. A **satnav** screen shows your road and the next turning, not every house. In a computer game, a **character** may be represented by a few values such as position, health and score rather than every cell in its body. In programs, a **variable name** stands in for a value, and a **function** hides how a task is done behind a simple name. In each case the user or programmer deals with a simpler idea.

bullets: Makes the problem **easier to understand** by removing distractions.
Reduces the **complexity** of the program and the amount of code.
Saves **memory and processing time** because irrelevant data is not stored or processed.
Allows **reuse**: a general solution can be applied to several similar problems.
Lets programmers use functions and libraries **without knowing how they work inside**.
Helps teams, since each person can focus on their own part.
Risk: if you remove **too much** detail, the solution may not work properly, so choose carefully.
core.p: Abstraction matters because real-world problems contain far too much detail to program directly. By focusing only on the **relevant** parts, a programmer **saves time**, produces **less complex code**, uses **less memory** and processing power for unnecessary data, and finds it easier to spot errors. Abstraction also allows a solution to be **reused**, because a general solution that ignores specific detail can be applied to many similar problems. It also makes it easier for different programmers to work together: one programmer can use a function without needing to know how it works inside.

bullets: Decomposition = **break a complex problem into smaller, simpler sub-problems**.
Each sub-problem can be **solved separately** and then combined.
Sub-problems can be **broken down further** until each is simple enough to program.
Often shown in a **structure diagram** (top-down design).
Leads naturally to **procedures and functions** (modular programming).
It is **not** hiding detail; that is abstraction.
Exam phrase: 'splitting a problem into smaller parts that are easier to solve'.
core.p: **Decomposition** is the process of **breaking a large, complex problem down into smaller, more manageable sub-problems**. Each sub-problem is simpler to solve than the whole, and if a sub-problem is still too big it can be broken down again. When every part has been solved, the parts are put back together to solve the original problem. Decomposition is sometimes shown in a **structure diagram**, which has the main problem at the top and the sub-problems branching downwards. It is the principle that explains why programs are written as **procedures and functions**.

bullets: Top level: **Quiz game**, the overall problem.
Second level: **Ask questions, Check answer, Keep score**.
Third level: pick question, show it, get answer, compare, add one, show total.
Each leaf box is **small enough to program and test** on its own.
The parts are **combined** at the end to form the finished program.
Structure diagrams are read **top to bottom**: the further down, the more detailed.
In an exam, draw boxes with **clear short labels** and **lines connecting parent and child**.
core.h: Decomposition: worked example and structure diagram
core.p: Consider writing a **quiz game**. The whole task is too large to tackle in one go, so decompose it: ask the questions, check the answers and keep the score. Each of these can be split again. Asking questions needs a way to pick a question and display it. Checking needs a way to get the player's answer and compare it with the correct one. Scoring needs a way to add a point and show the total. In the figure the top box is the problem and the bottom boxes are small, easy tasks that can each be written as a short subroutine. Different team members can then write different parts at the same time.

bullets: Each part is **simpler** to understand and design.
A team can **work in parallel** on different sub-problems.
Parts can be **tested separately**, making errors easier to find.
Good parts can be **reused** in other programs.
Individual modules can be **updated** without changing the whole program.
Makes **project management** easier: tasks can be assigned and tracked.
Disadvantage to be aware of: the parts must be **combined correctly**, so interfaces between them need careful planning.
core.p: Decomposition makes a big job manageable. Smaller parts are **easier to understand, design, program and test**. Several programmers can work on different parts **at the same time**, which speeds up the project, and each can specialise in the part they are best at. If something goes wrong, you can **test each part separately**, so errors are easier to **find and fix**. Parts that have been written once can be **reused** in other programs, and individual parts can be **improved or replaced** without rewriting everything. This is why large software projects are always built from many smaller modules.

bullets: Algorithmic thinking = **developing a precise step-by-step solution** to a problem.
An **algorithm** is an ordered set of instructions that solves a problem.
Must be **unambiguous**: each step has only one meaning.
Uses three building blocks: **sequence, selection, iteration**.
Identify **inputs, processes and outputs** first.
Algorithms are written in **pseudocode** or drawn as **flowcharts**, then converted into code.
Link to later topics: **trace tables** help you check an algorithm works.
core.p: **Algorithmic thinking** is the process of working out **a clear, step-by-step solution** to a problem, that is, an **algorithm**. An algorithm is a **sequence of precise instructions** that, if followed in order, solves a problem or completes a task. Algorithmic thinking means deciding what the **inputs** are, what **processing** must happen, what the **outputs** should be, and what **order** and **decisions (selection)** and **repetition (iteration)** are needed. The steps must be unambiguous so that a computer, which cannot guess, can follow them. Algorithms can be shown in **pseudocode** or **flowcharts** before being coded.

bullets: **Input**: data entering the system, for example a typed password or three test marks.
**Process**: what is done with the data, for example add and divide by 3, or compare with the stored password.
**Output**: the result, for example the mean, or a message 'access granted' or 'access denied'.
Identify IPO **before writing** pseudocode.
Questions may ask you to **list the inputs and outputs** of a described program.
Do not confuse process with output: **displaying** the answer is an output; **calculating** it is a process.
Link to the next topics: pseudocode, flowcharts and trace tables use the same ideas.
core.p: A key step in algorithmic thinking is to identify the **inputs, processes and outputs** of a problem. **Inputs** are the data that goes into the program, from the user, a file or a sensor. **Processes** are the calculations, comparisons and decisions the program performs on that data. **Outputs** are the results that are displayed, printed, stored or sent. Spotting these helps you decide which variables you need, what the program must do and what the result should look like. The figure shows two examples. Remember that a process may include **storing data** in variables or files as well as calculating.

bullets: **Abstraction**: keep only marks and the number of students; ignore names and other data.
**Decomposition**: input marks, calculate total, calculate average, display result.
**Algorithmic thinking**: total = 0, loop through every student adding their mark, then total divided by count.
**Input**: marks; **process**: addition and division; **output**: average mark.
Iteration (a loop) is needed because the same step is **repeated**.
Check the algorithm with a **small test** such as marks 4, 6 and 8: total 18, mean 6.
In answers, **name the principle** and **say what it does in the scenario**.
core.h: Computational thinking in a real example: a full walkthrough
core.p: Suppose a school wants a program that calculates and displays the **average mark** for a class test. **Abstraction**: the program only needs the students' marks, not their names, ages or lessons, so those details are ignored. **Decomposition**: split the task into get the marks, add them up, divide by the number of students, and display the result. **Algorithmic thinking**: decide the exact steps. Set a total to 0; for each student, input the mark and add it to the total; after the last student, divide the total by the number of students; output the answer. The three principles work together rather than separately, which is the point examiners want you to show.

bullets: **Abstraction** = hide detail (**what matters?**).
**Decomposition** = split the problem (**what are the parts?**).
**Algorithmic thinking** = plan the steps (**what order?**).
Memory aid: **hide, split, steps**.
They are usually used **together**, not in isolation.
Examples help: map (abstraction), structure diagram (decomposition), flowchart or pseudocode (algorithmic thinking).
In 'identify which principle' questions, look for the **key action** in the scenario: removing, splitting or sequencing.
core.p: Students often mix up the three principles, so learn to tell them apart quickly. **Abstraction** is about **what to ignore**: it removes detail and creates a simpler model. **Decomposition** is about **how to split**: it breaks the problem into parts. **Algorithmic thinking** is about **how to solve**: it produces the step-by-step instructions. A useful memory aid is **hide, split, steps**. In a typical project, a designer first abstracts the problem, then decomposes it into sub-problems, then writes an algorithm for each sub-problem, and finally codes and tests it, as shown in the pipeline figure.

bullets: 1 mark: **a correct definition** or one benefit.
2 marks: a definition **plus an example**, or a point with a reason.
3 to 4 marks: apply the principle to a scenario with **at least two specific sub-problems or details**.
Use the scenario's own nouns (for example 'the stock level', 'the customer's order').
Do **not** just repeat the question; add detail.
Do not write code unless asked; **describe or draw**.
Check that you have named the principle the question asks about.
core.h: Exam skills and command words for this topic
core.p: This topic produces short definition questions and longer application questions. For **'State what is meant by...'**, give a one-line definition using the key words. For **'Describe how...'** or **'Explain how decomposition could be used to...'**, you need to apply the idea to the scenario, naming specific sub-problems. For **'Give one benefit...'**, state a benefit and a reason. Use the exact terms in the specification (abstraction, decomposition, algorithmic thinking, input, process, output) and always relate your answer back to the program described. Practise drawing small structure diagrams and writing IPO tables so that you can do them quickly under timed conditions.

exam: **State/What is meant by (1 to 2 marks)**: use the key phrase. Abstraction: 'removing unnecessary detail'. Decomposition: 'breaking a problem into smaller parts'. Algorithmic thinking: 'a step-by-step solution'.
**Give one benefit (2 marks)**: a benefit plus a reason, for example 'Decomposition lets a team work on different parts at the same time, so the program is finished faster'.
**Identify the principle**: look at the scenario. Hiding detail is abstraction; splitting into parts is decomposition; writing out steps is algorithmic thinking.
**Describe how abstraction is used (3 marks)**: name what is ignored, what is kept and why, using the scenario's nouns.
**Describe how decomposition is used (3 to 4 marks)**: list at least two or three named sub-problems for the scenario.
**Inputs, processes and outputs**: write them in separate lists or a table; each correct item is typically one mark.
**Structure diagram questions**: put the main problem at the top, sub-problems below, joined with lines; keep labels short.
**Extended answers (6 marks)**: cover all three principles, apply them to the scenario and conclude how they help.
**Avoid** circular definitions such as 'abstraction is abstracting the problem'.
**Link to algorithms**: be ready to move from this topic into writing or completing pseudocode or flowcharts for the same scenario.

mistakes.r: That is decomposition. Abstraction is removing or hiding unnecessary detail to focus on what is important.
mistakes.w: Abstraction means breaking a problem into smaller parts.

mistakes.r: Decomposition is splitting a complex problem into smaller sub-problems that are easier to solve.
mistakes.w: Decomposition means removing the detail you don't need.

mistakes.r: An algorithm is a sequence of steps to solve a problem; a program is an algorithm written in a programming language.
mistakes.w: An algorithm is a computer program.

mistakes.r: It is working out the step-by-step solution, including order, decisions and repetition, before coding.
A process is something done to the data, such as a calculation; an output is the result shown or sent.
mistakes.w: Outputs are the same as processes.

mistakes.r: Apply the principle to the scenario by naming the specific details removed, sub-problems or steps.
mistakes.w: Giving a definition with no reference to the scenario in a 3 or 4 mark question.

mistakes.r: Abstraction makes it simpler by hiding unnecessary details, so it is easier to understand and program.
mistakes.w: Abstraction makes the problem more complicated.

mistakes.r: It helps with any problem by making it easier to understand, test and share between team members.
mistakes.w: Decomposition only helps with big programs.

summary: You must understand and apply the three principles of computational thinking, abstraction (hiding unnecessary detail), decomposition (breaking a problem into smaller parts) and algorithmic thinking (working out a step-by-step solution), and be able to identify inputs, processes and outputs and read structure diagrams. It matters because Paper 2 questions ask you to define them, apply them to a scenario and use them to plan programs.

terms.d: A set of problem-solving skills, including abstraction, decomposition and algorithmic thinking, used to solve problems in a way that a computer can carry out.
Removing or hiding unnecessary detail so that only the important features of a problem are considered.
Breaking a complex problem down into smaller, more manageable sub-problems.
Working out a precise step-by-step solution to a problem, including what order the steps must be in.
A sequence of steps, or set of instructions, that can be followed to complete a task or solve a problem.
Data that is entered into a system or program, for example from a keyboard, file or sensor.
An action carried out on data, such as a calculation, comparison or decision.
The result produced by a program, which can be displayed, printed, stored or sent.
A smaller part of a larger problem that is created by decomposition and can be solved separately.
A diagram that shows a problem broken down into sub-problems in a hierarchy, with the main problem at the top.
A simplified representation of a real-world situation that keeps only the relevant details.
Writing a program as separate sections, such as subroutines, each performing one task.
Instructions carried out one after another in a set order.
A decision in an algorithm where different instructions are followed depending on a condition.
Repeating a set of instructions, using a loop.
A way of writing an algorithm using structured, plain language that is not tied to a particular programming language.
A diagram that uses standard symbols and arrows to show the steps of an algorithm.

worked.ans: Decomposition means breaking the large problem of a booking system into smaller, more manageable sub-problems (1). For example the program could be split into choosing the film and showing time, selecting seats, taking the payment and producing the ticket (1). Each of these parts can be designed, programmed and tested separately (1), and different programmers can work on different parts at the same time, which makes the project quicker and errors easier to find (1).
worked.q: A company is creating a program to let customers book cinema tickets. Explain how decomposition could be used when developing this program. [4 marks]
steps: State what decomposition is: breaking the problem into smaller sub-problems.
Name at least three sub-problems in the scenario: choose film, choose seats, take payment, print or send ticket.
Say each can be solved or programmed separately.
Say why it helps: different programmers work at the same time, easier to test.

worked.ans: Abstraction (1). Unnecessary detail such as buildings and trees is removed so that only the important information, the route and the next turn, is shown (1). This makes the display easier to understand and means less data needs to be stored and processed (1).
worked.q: A satnav shows a simple line for the route and the next turn instead of every building and tree. Name the computational thinking principle being used and explain why it is helpful. [3 marks]
steps: State the benefit: driver can focus on the route and the program needs less data.

worked.ans: Input: the three test marks (1). Process: adding the three marks together and dividing the total by 3 (1). Output: the mean mark displayed to the user (1). For example, marks 4, 6 and 8 give 18 / 3 = 6.
worked.q: A program asks the user for three test marks and displays the mean. State the inputs, processes and outputs. [3 marks]
steps: Input: what is entered? Three marks.
Process: what is done? Add the marks, divide by 3.
Output: what is shown? The mean.
